questions.stem: Locate the median and the quartiles for the stem-and-leaf plot, and state the interquartile range (3|2 means 32).
questions.hint: n = 24 values. Median = average of the 12th and 13th values. Split into a lower half of 12 and an upper half of 12 to find Q1 and Q3.

steps.explain: Read the ordered data straight from the plot (leaves within each row are already ascending). There are n = 8 + 11 + 5 = 24 values.

n = 24 is even, so the median is the average of the 12th and 13th values. Counting through the rows (8, then 8+11=19, then 24), both fall in the stem-3 row: the 12th value is 32 and the 13th value is also 32.
Split the 24 values into a lower half (positions 1-12) and an upper half (positions 13-24), each of size 12 (even), so each quartile is the average of its half's two middle values.
steps.work: \(Q_1 = \dfrac{27+27}{2} = 27 \quad (\text{6th and 7th values})\)\\ \(Q_3 = \dfrac{38+39}{2} = 38.5 \quad (\text{6th and 7th values of the upper half})\)

steps.explain: Final answer: IQR = Q3 - Q1. Pitfall: misreading a stem-and-leaf row (e.g. treating "3 | 1 1 1" as one value 31 instead of three separate values 31, 31, 31) throws off every position count after it.

questions.stem: Here are two boxplots drawn on the same scale. Which data set has: the greater median? the greater range? the greater interquartile range? the greater largest data value?
options: greater median = A, greater range = B, greater IQR = B, greater max = B
greater median = B, greater range = B, greater IQR = B, greater max = B
greater median = A, greater range = A, greater IQR = B, greater max = B
greater median = A, greater range = B, greater IQR = A, greater max = B
questions.hint: Compare the median lines, the whisker-to-whisker spans (range), the box widths (IQR), and the right whisker ends (max), one at a time.
questions.solution: A has the greater median (32 vs 30); B has the greater range (33 vs 20), IQR (16 vs 7) and max (48 vs 40).

steps.explain: Compare the median (the line inside each box): Data set A's median is 32, Data set B's median is 30.
Compare the range (maximum - minimum) for each: A spans 20 to 40; B spans 15 to 48.
Compare the IQR (the width of each box, Q3 - Q1).

Final answer: compare the right whisker ends (maximum values). Pitfall: assuming the data set with the higher median must also have the greater max/range/IQR is a common but incorrect shortcut — each statistic must be checked separately.

questions.stem:
The heights, measured in centimetres, of 25 students in a class are:
170, 175, 133, 153, 164, 189, 143, 133, 167, 145, 150, 164, 169, 159, 177, 186, 173, 164, 177, 168, 142, 155, 153, 167, 166
. Which of these values are outliers, using the rule "a value is an outlier if it is more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) beyond the nearest quartile"?
questions.hint: Calculate the two outlier boundaries: \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\). Any value outside those boundaries is an outlier.
questions.solution: Lower bound = 151.5-30=121.5, upper bound = 171.5+30=201.5. min=133 and max=189 both lie inside these bounds, so there are no outliers.

steps.explain: State the outlier rule and calculate \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\).
Calculate the lower and upper outlier boundaries.
Check the actual minimum and maximum against these boundaries.

Final answer: since even the most extreme values (133 and 189) fall inside the boundaries, no value in this data set is an outlier. Pitfall: assuming the smallest and largest values are automatically outliers, without actually checking them against \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), is a common mistake.

questions.stem:
Using the same income data:
(Q1 = $67000, Q3 = $100000, IQR = $33000, minimum = $21000, maximum = $345000)
Which incomes are outliers?
questions.hint: Calculate the outlier boundaries \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), then check every unusually large or small value against them — not just the single maximum.
questions.solution: Lower bound = 67000-49500=17500, upper bound = 100000+49500=149500. Only 256000 and 345000 exceed the upper bound.

steps.explain: Calculate \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and the two outlier boundaries.
Check the minimum against the lower bound: $21000 is greater than $17500, so it is NOT an outlier.
Check every value above the upper bound of $149500. Scanning the ordered list, only two incomes exceed it.
Final answer: pitfall — outliers are not always just "the single highest or lowest value"; here TWO separate incomes both exceed the upper boundary.

Identify any outliers.
questions.hint: Calculate \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), and check the minimum and maximum against them.
questions.solution: Lower bound = 32.5-17.25=15.25, upper bound = 44+17.25=61.25. min=22>15.25 (not outlier). max=62>61.25, so 62 IS an outlier.

steps.explain: Calculate \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and the outlier boundaries.
Check the minimum against the lower bound.
Check the maximum against the upper bound.
Final answer: pitfall — 62 only just clears the boundary (61.25), so it is easy to wrongly dismiss it as "not extreme enough"; always compare the exact numbers rather than eyeballing.

Press AC to finish entering all 20 values, then open the statistics variable menu and select \(\bar{x}\) to read the mean.

Final answer: the calculator gives the mean directly. Pitfall: this is NOT the same as the median (which the calculator would give under a different STAT variable, and equals 31.00 here) — mean and median only coincide for perfectly symmetric data.

questions.hint: First find the mean using your calculator's statistics mode (e.g. Casio fx-82AU PLUS). Then add up the frequencies for every score strictly less than that mean.
questions.solution: On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: MODE → STAT → 1-VAR gives x̄ = 6.15. Scores 0-6 have frequencies 0,2,0,1,1,2,4 which sum to 10.

steps.explain: Put the calculator into statistics mode to find the mean. On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: press MODE, then select STAT (usually "2"), then select 1-VAR (usually "1"). Turn on the frequency column first if it is not already showing: SHIFT → MODE (SETUP) → STAT → Frequency: On.

Press AC to finish entering data, then open the statistics variable menu and select \(\bar{x}\) to read the mean directly off the calculator.
Now use this mean to identify which scores are less than it — this includes every score from 0 up to and including 6.
Add up the frequencies for each of these scores (either by hand from the table, or by reading the FREQ column back off the calculator's STAT table).

questions.solution: On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: MODE → STAT → 1-VAR, turn Frequency on, enter each score/frequency pair, then read x̄ = 6.15 and σx ≈ 2.46 from SHIFT 1 (STAT) → Var.

steps.explain: Put the calculator into statistics mode. On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: press MODE, then select STAT (usually "2"), then select 1-VAR (usually "1"). This opens a table with an X column ready for data entry.

Turn on the frequency column so you can enter each score once along with how many people got it, instead of typing a score in repeatedly. Press SHIFT then MODE (SETUP), scroll down to STAT, and turn Frequency ON. Re-enter STAT mode afterwards if needed.

Enter each score in the X column and its frequency in the FREQ column, pressing \(=\) after each entry to move to the next row. Only scores with a non-zero frequency need a row (skip scores 2 and 8, which had 0 people).
steps.work: \(X: 0,1,3,4,5,6,7,9,10\)\\ \(\text{FREQ}: 2,1,1,2,4,6,2,2\)\\ (\text{score } 0 \text{ has FREQ } 0, \text{ so it can be skipped too})

steps.explain: Press AC to finish entering data and return to the calculation screen. Open the statistics variable menu.

From the Var menu, select \(\bar{x}\) to display the mean, and \(=\) to confirm it matches the given mean of 6.15. Then reopen SHIFT 1 → Var and select \(\sigma x\) (the population standard deviation — NOT \(sx\), which uses n-1 and is a different value this course does not use).

Final answer: the calculator gives the standard deviation directly. Pitfall: selecting \(sx\) instead of \(\sigma x\) on the Var menu divides by n-1=19 instead of n=20, giving the close-but-wrong distractor 2.52 — always check which symbol you are reading.

questions.stem: Thirty randomly chosen passengers at Sydney Airport were surveyed about the length of time in minutes they spent waiting in line at Customs. The data is shown in the stem-and-leaf plot below  If the range of the scores is 44, find the value of \(\Delta\).
questions.hint: Range = highest value - lowest value. Read the lowest value from the stem 0 row first.
questions.solution: Range = 44, minimum = 5, so maximum = 49 = 40 + Delta, giving Delta = 9.

steps.explain: Identify the known values: this is a stem-and-leaf plot where each entry is read as stem × 10 + leaf. We are told the range of all 30 scores is 44, and asked to find the missing leaf \(\Delta\) in the last row (stem 4).

Read the minimum value directly off the plot: the smallest stem is 0, and its smallest leaf is 5, so the minimum score is 5. Pitfall: do not read the stem digit "0" itself as the minimum — you must combine it with its smallest leaf.
The maximum score must be in the last row (stem 4), since every earlier row has a smaller stem. Its value is \(40 + \Delta\). Use the range formula to solve for the maximum, then for \(\Delta\).
Final answer: substituting back confirms 49 - 5 = 44, which matches the given range.

questions.stem:
Using the same stem-and-leaf plot of Customs waiting times (\(\Delta = 9\)):

Find the median waiting time.
questions.hint: There are 30 values (even), so the median is the average of the 15th and 16th values once the data is in ascending order.
questions.solution: The 15th value is 32 and the 16th value is 34, so the median is 33.

steps.explain: A stem-and-leaf plot already lists leaves in ascending order within each row, so the full data set (n = 30) is already ordered once you read row by row. Count how many values fall in each row: 4, 5, 5, 9, 7.

Since n = 30 is even, the median is the average of the \(\frac{n}{2} = 15\)th and \(\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right) = 16\)th values. Count cumulatively through the rows to locate them: after stem 0 (4 values), stem 1 (9 values), stem 2 (14 values), the 15th and 16th values fall inside the stem 3 row.
Row 3 (stem 3) in order is 32, 34, 34, 36, 37, 37, 38, 39, 39 — these are positions 15 to 23. So the 15th value is 32 and the 16th value is 34.
Average the two middle values to get the median. Pitfall: forgetting to average when n is even, and just picking one of the two middle values, is a common mistake.

questions.stem:
For the following set of scores, determine the mean:
17, 27, 37, 40, 28, 35, 37, 20
questions.hint: Mean = (sum of all scores) / (number of scores). Count the scores carefully — there are 8 of them.

steps.explain: Identify the data set and count how many scores there are (n = 8): 17, 27, 37, 40, 28, 35, 37, 20. We need the mean, \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\).
Add all the scores together carefully, keeping a running total.
Divide the total by n = 8. Pitfall: a very common mistake is miscounting the number of scores (e.g. using n = 7 or n = 9), which is exactly how two of the other options were produced.
Final answer: the mean of the data set is 30.125.

questions.stem:
For the following set of scores, determine the standard deviation (to 2 decimal places):
17, 27, 37, 40, 28, 35, 37, 20
(The mean of this data set is 30.125.)
questions.hint: Standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}\). Square each deviation before adding them — don't forget the square root at the end.
questions.solution: sum of squared deviations = 504.875, divided by n = 8 gives variance 63.109, sqrt gives SD approx 7.94.

steps.explain: State the formula for standard deviation (population version, used in this course) and the known mean \(\bar{x} = 30.125\), n = 8.
Find each deviation from the mean, \(x - \bar{x}\), for all 8 scores.

Square every deviation (this removes the negative signs) and add them together. Pitfall: forgetting to square the deviations, or squaring but forgetting the final square root, gives the wrong-looking large distractor (63.11) — that is the variance, not the standard deviation.

Divide by n = 8 to get the variance, then take the square root. Pitfall: dividing by \(n - 1 = 7\) instead of n = 8 gives a slightly different (wrong, for this course's definition) answer of about 8.49.

questions.hint: Split the ordered data into a lower half (first 15 values) and an upper half (last 15 values). \(Q_1\) is the median of the lower half, \(Q_3\) is the median of the upper half. \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\).
questions.solution: Q1 = 18 (median of first 15 values), Q3 = 39 (median of last 15 values), IQR = 39 - 18 = 21.

steps.explain: With n = 30 values already ordered, split the data into two equal halves of 15 values each: the lower half and the upper half.
\(Q_1\) is the median of the lower half. With 15 values, the median is the 8th value.

\(Q_3\) is the median of the upper half. Again, with 15 values, the median is the 8th value of that half. Pitfall: mixing up which half gives \(Q_1\) vs \(Q_3\), or using the whole 30-value list's 8th/23rd value instead of splitting first, are common errors here.
The interquartile range is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles. Pitfall: the range (44) is a different statistic — don't confuse "range" with "interquartile range".

Find the range and interquartile range of the data set:

n = 9 is odd, so the median (10) sits alone in the middle. Omit it and split the rest into a lower half of 4 and an upper half of 4. \(Q_1\) is the median of the lower half; \(Q_3\) is the median of the upper half.

questions.stem:
Find the mean, the mode, the median and the interquartile range of this data set.
Value 012345678910
Frequency 520718460211
questions.hint: n = sum of the frequencies. Mean = (sum of value x frequency) / n. Mode = the value with the highest frequency (not the frequency itself). Use cumulative frequencies to locate the median and quartiles.

steps.explain: Find n by adding all the frequencies, and find the total by adding value x frequency for each row.

Mean = total / n. Mode = the value with the highest frequency — here the highest frequency is 11 (belonging to value 10), so the mode is 10, not 11. Pitfall: confusing the mode (the value) with its frequency (the count) is exactly how the second option was produced.

Build cumulative frequencies to locate the median (n = 46 even, so average the 23rd and 24th values): value 0 reaches cumulative 5, value 1 reaches 7, value 3 reaches 14, value 4 reaches 15, value 5 reaches 23, value 6 reaches 27. The 23rd value is 5 (last one at value 5) and the 24th value is 6 (first one at value 6).

Q1 is the median of the lower 23 values (12th value overall): cumulative frequency reaches value 3 by position 14, so position 12 is inside value 3, giving Q1 = 3. Q3 is the median of the upper 23 values (35th value overall): cumulative frequency reaches value 9 by position 35, so Q3 = 9. Final answer: IQR = Q3 - Q1.

The following marks were scored by 9 students in a test:
0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 6, 8
Two students were absent and did the test on a later day. When their marks were included, the mean stayed the same but the mode changed. What could their marks have been?
questions.hint: First find the original mean, then use "mean stays the same" to find what the two new marks must add up to. Finally check each option to see whether the mode actually changes.
questions.solution: Original mean = 3, so the two new marks must sum to 6. Only 3 and 3 changes the mode from 2 to 3.

steps.explain: Find the mean and mode of the original 9 marks: 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 6, 8.
Adding two more students makes n = 11. "The mean stayed the same" means the mean is still 3, so use this to find the required new total, then the sum of the two new marks.
steps.work: \(\text{new sum} = \bar{x} \times n = 3 \times 11 = 33\)\\ \(\text{sum of the two new marks} = 33 - 27 = 6\)

steps.explain: Every option given adds to 6 (0+6, 1+5, 3+3, 2+4), so the mean condition alone cannot distinguish them. Check each option against the second condition: does adding it make the mode change from 2?
steps.work: \(0,6: \text{counts become } 2{:}3,\ 3{:}2,\ 0{:}2,\ 6{:}2 \Rightarrow \text{mode still } 2\)\\ \(1,5: \text{counts become } 2{:}3,\ 3{:}2 \Rightarrow \text{mode still } 2\)\\ \(2,4: \text{counts become } 2{:}4 \Rightarrow \text{mode still } 2 \ (\text{just more common})\)\\ \(3,3: \text{counts become } 3{:}4,\ 2{:}3 \Rightarrow \text{mode becomes } 3\)

steps.explain: Only adding 3 and 3 both keeps the mean at 3 AND changes the mode (from 2 to 3). Pitfall: many students stop after checking the mean and pick any pair that sums to 6 — the mode condition is what actually decides the answer.

Rearrange to make \(x\) the subject, then substitute the known values in.
Carry out the multiplication first, then add. Pitfall: adding the mean and SD first (55 + 6 = 61, then multiplying by z) gives the wrong order of operations and a wrong answer.
Final answer: Di's actual mark was 73, which is 3 standard deviations above the mean.

questions.solution: z(Maths) = 0.5, z(English) = 1.0, so English is the relatively better result.

steps.explain: Comparing raw scores directly (77 in Maths vs 70 in English) is meaningless here, because the two subjects have different means and spreads. Each score must be converted to a z-score using its own subject's mean and SD.
Calculate the z-score for Maths, using Maths' own mean (70) and SD (14).
Calculate the z-score for English, using English's own mean (60) and SD (10). Pitfall: using the wrong subject's mean/SD (e.g. Maths' SD for English) is a common mix-up.

The higher z-score represents the better result relative to the rest of the cohort, regardless of which raw score is numerically bigger. questions.solution: Each quarter of the data (25%) sits between consecutive markers: min-Q1, Q1-median, median-Q3, Q3-max.

steps.explain: Quartiles are defined so that each of the four sections of the ordered data — minimum to Q1, Q1 to median, median to Q3, and Q3 to maximum — contains approximately 25% of the data.
Below the median means the first two sections combined (min to Q1, plus Q1 to median).
Below the lower quartile is just the first section on its own.

The box covers Q1 to Q3 (the middle two sections combined = 50%); each whisker covers one outer section on its own (25% each). Pitfall: confusing "in the box" (50%, two sections) with "below the lower quartile" (25%, one section) is the most common mix-up.

questions.stem: In a boxplot, is one whisker always longer than the other?
options: Yes — the right-hand whisker is always longer, because real data is usually positively skewed.
Yes — both whiskers are always exactly equal, because the median splits the box in half.
Yes — the left-hand whisker is always longer, because the minimum is always further from Q1 than the maximum is from Q3.
No — the relative whisker lengths depend entirely on how the data is spread near the minimum and maximum; either whisker can be longer, shorter, or the two can be equal.
questions.hint: Whisker length depends on the gap between Q1 and the minimum, and between Q3 and the maximum — these gaps are set by the actual data values, not by any rule.
questions.solution: No fixed rule forces one whisker to be longer — it depends entirely on the data's distribution near its extremes.

steps.explain: The left whisker length is (Q1 - minimum); the right whisker length is (maximum - Q3). Both are determined purely by how the most extreme 25% of values on each side happen to be spread out.

A symmetric data set tends to have similar whisker lengths; a data set with an unusually spread-out tail on one side (positive or negative skew) will have a longer whisker on that side. The "Symmetric example" below has equal 20-unit whiskers on both sides; the "Skewed example" has a short 4-unit left whisker but a long 25-unit right whisker.
steps.work: \(\text{skewed right (positive skew)} \Rightarrow \text{right whisker often longer}\)\\ \(\text{skewed left (negative skew)} \Rightarrow \text{left whisker often longer}\)

steps.explain: Since either pattern (or a symmetric one with equal whiskers) is possible depending on the actual data, no single option ("always the right", "always equal", "always the left") can be a universal rule.
Final answer: no, one whisker is not always longer — it depends on the shape/skew of the specific data set.
steps.work: \(\text{whisker length depends on data spread near the extremes}\)

questions.solution:
Q1 = 13 (median of the lower 5 values: 10,12,13,14,14), median = 15 (6th value), Q3 = 30 (median of the upper 5 values: 20,25,30,40,50).

The gap from Q1 to the median is only 15 - 13 = 2, while the gap from the median to Q3 is 30 - 15 = 15 — nowhere near equal, so the median sits well off-centre, close to the Q1 side of the box.

This happens because the median splits the data into two halves with an EQUAL NUMBER of values on each side (5 and 5), but that does not mean those halves are equally spread out. Here the lower half (10 to 14) is tightly clustered in a narrow range, while the upper half (20 to 50) is spread out over a much wider range — so even though exactly 25% of the data lies in each of the two sections next to the median, one section is visually much narrower than the other.

steps.explain: Order the 11 values (already given in order) and find n.
n = 11 is odd, so the median is the single middle value, at position \(\frac{11+1}{2}=6\).
Remove the median and split the remaining 10 values into a lower half of 5 and an upper half of 5. Each half has an odd size, so its median is its own single middle (3rd) value.

Compare the two gaps either side of the median: (median - Q1) versus (Q3 - median). If they are very different, the median sits off-centre in the box, closer to whichever quartile has the smaller gap.
steps.work: \(\text{median} - Q_1 = 15 - 13 = 2\)\\ \(Q_3 - \text{median} = 30 - 15 = 15\)\\ \(2 \ll 15 \Rightarrow \text{median is close to } Q_1\text{, far from } Q_3\)

Compare the right whisker ends (maximum marks obtained).

Final answer: compare the left whisker ends (minimum marks obtained). Pitfall: Class A having the higher median does NOT mean Class A did better on every measure — B has more variability (higher IQR) and a wider overall spread (both the highest and the lowest mark).

questions.stem: Using the same two classes' boxplots, which class did better on the test? Give reasons for your choice. (Class discussion)

questions.solution: Reasonable answer: Class A did better "typically" — its median (35) is higher than Class B's (32), and its smaller IQR (8 vs 14) shows Class A's marks were more consistent/tightly clustered around a solid result. However, Class B contains both the single highest mark (48) and the single lowest mark (15), so a case can also be made for Class B having more high achievers, at the cost of more students struggling. Either answer is acceptable if backed by the correct statistics.

questions.hint: IQR = Q3 - Q1 for each channel. Compare the three box widths.
questions.solution: IQR(A)=6, IQR(B)=9, IQR(C)=2.5. Channel B has the largest IQR.

steps.explain: Calculate the IQR for each channel: IQR = Q3 - Q1.
Compare the three values — the IQR is visually the width of each box, so this can also be checked directly on the plot.

Pitfall: it is tempting to assume the channel with the largest range (max - min) also has the largest IQR, but Channel A has a slightly larger range than Channel B (17 vs 14) while having a smaller IQR — the two statistics measure different things.

questions.solution: max(A)=25, max(B)=23, max(C)=20. So A > B > C.

Match each maximum back to its channel.

questions.solution: median(A)=16, median(B)=18, median(C)=16.5. So B > C > A.

steps.explain: Read each channel's median directly from the line inside its box.
Order the three medians from largest to smallest.

Match each median back to its channel. Pitfall: Channel A had the highest-rated single program (Q11c), but that does not mean it also has the largest median — a channel can have one outstanding hit show while typically rating lower than its rivals.
Final answer: rank from highest to lowest median.

questions.stem: Using the same TV channel boxplots, can you find a criterion that makes Channel C the winning channel?
questions.hint: Channel C does not win on median (B is higher) or on maximum single-program rating (A is higher). Look at what Channel C's narrow box tells you about its programs instead.
questions.solution: Channel C has by far the smallest interquartile range (2.5, vs 6 for A and 9 for B) and the highest lower quartile (Q1 = 15, vs 13 for A and 12 for B). So a criterion like "most consistent channel" (smallest IQR) or "channel whose worst-rated 75% of programs still rate the highest" (highest Q1) makes Channel C the winner — even though it never has a single standout hit show, it never has a real flop either.

questions.stem:
Three histograms (a, b, c) and three boxplots (i, ii, iii), all on the same scale, describe the same three data sets. Histogram a is a symmetric bell shape peaking in the middle. Histogram b has bars increasing in height from left to right (most data concentrated at the high end, with a thin tail toward the low end). Histogram c has bars decreasing in height from left to right (most data concentrated at the low end, with a thin tail toward the high end).
Match each histogram to its boxplot and describe the shape of each distribution.
options: a-iii (symmetric); b-i (negatively skewed — box shifted high, outliers toward the low end); c-ii (positively skewed — box shifted low, outliers toward the high end)
questions.hint: A symmetric histogram matches a boxplot with roughly equal whiskers and no outliers. A histogram with a thin tail on one side matches a boxplot whose box is shifted toward the opposite (bulk) side, with outliers appearing on the thin-tail side.
questions.solution: a matches iii (symmetric); b (bulk high, tail low) is negatively skewed, matching i; c (bulk low, tail high) is positively skewed, matching ii.

steps.explain: Histogram a is a symmetric bell shape, so its boxplot should have a box roughly centred with two whiskers of similar length and no outliers — this matches boxplot iii.

Histogram b has most of its data concentrated at the HIGH end, with only a thin tail stretching toward the low end. A distribution with a long thin tail toward low values is called negatively skewed. Its boxplot should have the box shifted toward the high end, with any outliers appearing on the low side.
steps.work: \(b \to i \ (\text{negatively skewed: tail toward low values})\)

steps.explain: Histogram c has most of its data concentrated at the LOW end, with a thin tail stretching toward the high end. This is called positively skewed. Its boxplot should have the box shifted toward the low end, with any outliers appearing on the high side.
steps.work: \(c \to ii \ (\text{positively skewed: tail toward high values})\)

steps.explain: Final answer: match all three pairs and their shape descriptions together. Pitfall: it is very common to swap "positively skewed" and "negatively skewed" — the skew direction refers to which side has the long thin TAIL, not which side has the bulk of the data.

questions.stem:
Consider the data shown in the stem-and-leaf plot (17|0 means 170):

Stem | Leaf
15 | 6 8
16 | 9 9
17 | 0 1 3 3 4 5 8 8 9 9
18 | 0 0 1 3 3 4 7 7 8 8
19 | 1 2 3

If this data is grouped into a histogram with class width 10 (150-159, 160-169, etc.), which class interval(s) have the highest frequency?
questions.hint: Count how many leaves are in each stem row — each stem row IS one class interval when the class width matches the stem.
questions.solution: Row counts: 150s=2, 160s=2, 170s=10, 180s=10, 190s=3. The two highest (tied) are 170-179 and 180-189.

steps.explain: Since the class width (10) matches the stem, each stem row is exactly one histogram class. Count the leaves in each row.
Compare all five frequencies to find the highest.
Two classes are tied for the highest frequency. Pitfall: assuming only one class can "win" and picking just one of the tied classes is a common mistake — always check for ties.
Final answer: both 170-179 and 180-189 have the highest frequency, 10.

Stem | Leaf

18 | 0 0 1 3 3 4 7 7 8 8

steps.explain: Read the ordered data from the plot: n = 2+2+10+10+3 = 27 values.
n = 27 is odd, so the median is the single middle value at position \(\frac{27+1}{2} = 14\). Counting cumulatively (2, 4, 14), the 14th value is the last leaf of the stem-17 row.

Remove the median and split the remaining 26 values into a lower half of 13 (positions 1-13) and an upper half of 13 (positions 15-27). Each half is odd-sized, so its median is its own single middle (7th) value.
steps.work: \(Q_1 = 7\text{th value of lower half} = 173\)\\ \(Q_3 = 7\text{th value of upper half} = 187\)

steps.explain: Final answer: IQR = Q3 - Q1.

(min = 156, Q1 = 173, median = 179, Q3 = 187, max = 193, IQR = 14)
Are there any outliers?
questions.hint: Calculate \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), then compare the actual minimum and maximum to those boundaries.
questions.solution: Lower bound = 173-21=152, upper bound = 187+21=208. min=156 and max=193 both lie within these bounds, so there are no outliers.

steps.explain: Calculate \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and the outlier boundaries.
Compare the actual minimum and maximum against the boundaries.
Since both extreme values fall inside the boundaries, neither is an outlier.

questions.stem: Comment on the shape of the histogram and boxplot for this data (class frequencies: 150s=2, 160s=2, 170s=10, 180s=10, 190s=3; min=156, Q1=173, median=179, Q3=187, max=193, no outliers).
options: Approximately symmetric — the two tallest classes (170s and 180s) sit either side of the median, with roughly matching small classes at both ends.
Strongly positively skewed — most of the data is concentrated at the low end with a long tail toward high values.
Strongly negatively skewed — most of the data is concentrated at the high end with a long tail toward low values.
Uniform — every class has approximately the same frequency.
questions.hint: Compare the class frequencies on either side of the median, and compare the two whisker lengths (Q1 - min) vs (max - Q3).
questions.solution: Frequencies rise to a peak around 170-189 then fall off similarly on both sides; whisker lengths (173-156=17) and (193-187=6) are roughly comparable given the small tail counts — overall a roughly symmetric shape.

steps.explain: Look at the histogram frequencies: they rise from 2 (150s) to 10 (170s and 180s, tied) then fall to 3 (190s) — a rise-then-fall shape typical of a roughly symmetric or bell-shaped distribution, not a one-directional skew.
Check the boxplot whisker lengths, which should be roughly comparable for a symmetric distribution.

While the whiskers are not perfectly equal, both the histogram shape (peak in the middle two classes with small tails on both sides) and the fact there are no outliers on either side both point away from a strong skew.
steps.work: \(\text{peak near the centre, small tails both sides}\)

steps.explain: Final answer: this data set is best described as approximately symmetric.

questions.stem: The lower and upper quartiles for a data set are 116 and 134. Which of the following data values would be classified as an outlier: 190, 60, or 150?
questions.hint: IQR = 134 - 116 = 18. Calculate both boundaries, \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), and check each value individually.
questions.solution: IQR=18. Bounds: 116-27=89, 134+27=161. 190>161 (outlier). 60<89 (outlier). 150 is between 89 and 161 (not an outlier).

steps.explain: Calculate the IQR and \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\).
Calculate the two outlier boundaries.
Check each of the three values against the boundaries individually.
Final answer: pitfall — 150 might look "large" at a glance, but it is well inside the upper boundary of 161, so it is not an outlier.

find Q1, the median, Q3 and the IQR (for the boxplot).

(min = 3, Q1 = 18.5, median = 26.5, Q3 = 34, max = 51). Comment on the shape of the distribution.

Perfectly symmetric — both whiskers are exactly equal in length.

questions.solution: left whisker = 18.5-3=15.5, right whisker = 51-34=17. The right whisker is slightly longer, indicating a mild positive skew.

Compare the two lengths.
A slightly longer right (upper) whisker suggests a mild positive skew — a small tail of higher speed values (like 40, 42, 51) stretching the data upward.

8, 5, 10, 6, 6, 12, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, 13, 7, 7, 7, 6, 6, 4, 5, 5
If this data is displayed as a dotplot, what is the mode (or modes)?
options: 5 kg and 6 kg (bimodal — both occur 5 times)
questions.hint: Tally how many times each weight-loss value occurs. There can be more than one mode if two values tie for the highest frequency.
questions.solution: Tally: 4->2, 5->5, 6->5, 7->3, 8->2, 10->1, 12->1, 13->1. Both 5 and 6 tie for the highest count (5 each).

steps.explain: Tally how many times each value appears in the data set.
The mode is the value (or values) with the highest frequency. Here, 5 and 6 are tied with a frequency of 5 each — higher than any other value.
A data set can have more than one mode — this is called bimodal.
Final answer: pitfall — stopping the tally early or miscounting one value (e.g. thinking 6 appears 6 times) can hide the tie and make it look like there is a single mode.

find Q1, the median, Q3 and the IQR for the boxplot.

Split into a lower half of 10 (positions 1-10) and an upper half of 10 (positions 11-20).

questions.stem:

(min = 4, Q1 = 5, median = 6, Q3 = 7.5, max = 13, IQR = 2.5)

questions.solution: Bounds: 5-3.75=1.25, 7.5+3.75=11.25. 12 and 13 exceed the upper bound (outliers). The long right whisker/tail (up to 13) vs short left side shows positive skew.

steps.explain: Calculate the outlier boundaries.
Check the extreme values against the boundaries.

Compare the general spread on each side of the median: most values cluster tightly between 4 and 8, with just a couple of much larger values (10, 12, 13) stretching the data upward — a tail toward high values.
steps.work: \(\text{most data in } [4,8], \text{ few high values up to } 13\)

The number of kicks obtained by a football player each week over a season is:
18, 18, 20, 26, 10, 8, 21, 14, 16, 14, 12, 16
Calculate the mean number of kicks obtained by the player.
questions.hint: Mean = (sum of all values) / (number of values). Count the values carefully — there are 12.

steps.explain: Identify the data set and count the number of values, n = 12.
Add all 12 values together.

Divide the total by n = 12. Pitfall: it is easy to accidentally miscount how many values are in the list, or to confuse the mean with the median (the middle value once ordered) — the median here is 16.00, a different number entirely.

questions.stem:
The daily maximum temperature was recorded in two different cities for a week:

| City | Day 1 | Day 2 | Day 3 | Day 4 | Day 5 | Day 6 | Day 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 28 | 31 | 34 | 32 | 31 | 29 | 28 |
| B | 26 | 32 | 36 | 38 | 37 | 29 | 25 |

Which city had the greater mean daily maximum temperature?
options: City A (30.43 > 31.86 is false — City B is actually greater)
They are equal, since both means round to 31
questions.hint: Calculate the mean of each city's 7 temperatures separately, then compare.
questions.solution: mean(A) = 213/7 ≈ 30.43. mean(B) = 223/7 ≈ 31.86. City B has the greater mean.

steps.explain: Calculate the mean of City A's temperatures.
Calculate the mean of City B's temperatures.
Compare the two means directly.
Final answer: City B had the greater mean daily maximum temperature.

questions.stem: The average of 5 masses is 67 kg. If a mass of 25 kg is added, what is the average of the 6 masses?
questions.hint: First find the total of the original 5 masses (mean × count). Add the new mass to that total, then divide by the new count (6).
questions.solution: Original total = 67×5 = 335. New total = 335+25 = 360. New average = 360/6 = 60.

steps.explain: Find the total of the original 5 masses using mean = total / count.
Add the new mass (25 kg) to the total.
Divide the new total by the new count of masses, 6. Pitfall: dividing by the OLD count (5) instead of the new count (6) is a common mistake, and just averaging the two numbers 67 and 25 is another.
Final answer: the average of the 6 masses is 60 kg.

questions.stem: During a term, a student has an average of 46 marks after the first four tests, and an average of 38 marks for the next six tests. What is the student's average for all ten tests?
questions.hint: Find the total marks from each group of tests separately (mean × count for each group), add the totals, then divide by the total number of tests (10). Do NOT just average the two given averages — the groups have different sizes.

steps.explain: Find the total marks from the first four tests.
Find the total marks from the next six tests.
Add the two totals together to get the total marks across all ten tests.

Final answer: divide by the total number of tests, 10. Pitfall: simply averaging 46 and 38 to get 42 ignores that the two groups have different sizes (4 tests vs 6 tests) — a weighted average is needed, not a plain average of the two means.

questions.stem:
Calculate, correct to two decimal places, the mean and standard deviation for the data set:
2, 4, 8, 10, 2, 9, 3, 8, 2, 2
questions.hint: Use your calculator's statistics mode (e.g. Casio fx-82AU PLUS): enter all 10 values as individual \(x\)-entries, then read \(\bar{x}\) and \(\sigma x\) directly from the STAT variable menu.
questions.solution: On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: MODE → STAT → 1-VAR, enter all 10 values, then read x̄ = 5.00 and σx ≈ 3.16 from SHIFT 1 (STAT) → Var.

steps.explain: Put the calculator into statistics mode. On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: press MODE, then select STAT (usually "2"), then select 1-VAR (usually "1"). This opens a table with an X column ready for data entry.

Enter each of the 10 values into the X column in order, pressing \(=\) after every value to move to the next row. Repeated values (like 2, which occurs four times) are simply typed in again each time.
Press AC to finish entering all 10 values, then open the statistics variable menu and select \(\bar{x}\) to read the mean.
Reopen the same menu and select \(\sigma x\) (the population standard deviation — NOT \(sx\), which divides by n-1 and is a different value this course does not use).

Final answer: the calculator gives both statistics directly. Pitfall: reading off the variance display (10.00) instead of the standard deviation display, or selecting \(sx\) instead of \(\sigma x\) (which would give 3.33), are both common mix-ups.

questions.stem:
Two data sets are given below:

| Data set i | 2 | 4 | 8 | 10 | 2 | 9 | 3 | 8 | 2 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data set ii | 3 | 6 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 6 |

Both have mean = 5.00. Data set i has \(\sigma \approx 3.16\); data set ii has \(\sigma \approx 1.34\). What can be concluded by comparing them?
options: Data set i is more tightly clustered around the mean than data set ii.
The two data sets have different means, so they cannot be compared.
Both data sets are spread out from the mean by about the same amount.
Both data sets have the same mean, but data set ii is much more tightly clustered around it than data set i.
questions.hint: A larger standard deviation means the data is more spread out from the mean; a smaller standard deviation means it is more tightly clustered.
questions.solution: Both means are 5.00, but sigma(i)=3.16 is much larger than sigma(ii)=1.34, so data set ii is far more tightly clustered around the shared mean.

steps.explain: Compare the two means first — they are identical (both 5.00), so the "centre" of both data sets is the same.
Compare the two standard deviations, which measure spread around that shared mean.
Since \(\sigma_i > \sigma_{ii}\), data set i is more spread out from the mean, and data set ii is more tightly clustered around it.
Final answer: same mean, but very different spread — this is exactly the kind of comparison the standard deviation is designed to reveal, which the mean alone cannot show.

questions.stem:

| \(x_i\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |

questions.solution: On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: MODE → STAT → 1-VAR, turn Frequency on, enter each x/f pair, then read x̄ = 3.00 and σx ≈ 1.45 from SHIFT 1 (STAT) → Var.

questions.stem: For the data set 4, 7, 13, calculate the mean and show that the sum of the deviations \((x - \bar{x})\) is zero. Then show algebraically that this must be true for ANY three numbers \(a, b, c\) with mean \(\bar{x}\).
questions.hint: First find the mean of 4, 7, 13 and check the three deviations add to zero. Then repeat the same steps using letters instead of numbers: write \(\bar{x}\) in terms of a, b, c, substitute it into \((a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x})\), and simplify.
questions.solution: Numeric check: mean = (4+7+13)/3 = 8. Deviations: 4-8=-4, 7-8=-1, 13-8=5. Sum = -4-1+5 = 0. General proof: \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\), so \(3\bar{x}=a+b+c\). Sum of deviations \(= (a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x}) = (a+b+c) - 3\bar{x} = 3\bar{x} - 3\bar{x} = 0\), for any values of a, b and c.

steps.explain: Calculate the mean of the concrete data set 4, 7, 13.
Calculate each deviation from the mean, and add them together.
Now repeat the same idea using letters a, b, c instead of 4, 7, 13, so the result holds for ANY three numbers, not just this one example. Write the mean in terms of a, b, c.
Final answer: expand the sum of the three deviations and substitute \(a+b+c = 3\bar{x}\) from the previous step.

questions.stem: Prove that the sum of the deviations of any data set (with n values \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and mean \(\bar{x}\)) is zero.
questions.hint: Use the general definition \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\), and expand \(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})\) using summation properties.
questions.solution: \(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - \sum_{i=1}^n \bar{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - n\bar{x}\). Since \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\), we have \(n\bar{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\), so the expression equals \(\sum x_i - \sum x_i = 0\) for any data set.

steps.explain: This is the exact same idea as the previous question (where you checked it for 3 numbers, a, b, c), now written for ANY number of values, n. State the mean formula and what "sum of the deviations" means in summation notation: it is \(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})\), i.e. \((x_1-\bar{x}) + (x_2-\bar{x}) + \cdots + (x_n-\bar{x})\) added together.

Split the sum into two separate sums — one of the \(x_i\) values, and one of the \(\bar{x}\) values. This is allowed because summation distributes over subtraction, exactly like \((x_1+x_2) - (y_1+y_2) = (x_1-y_1)+(x_2-y_2)\) rearranged.

Simplify the second sum. \(\bar{x}\) is a single fixed number (the mean), not something that changes with i, so adding it to itself n times (once for each of the n data values) just gives \(n\bar{x}\).

Substitute this back in. The expression becomes \(\sum x_i - n\bar{x}\). Now use the definition of the mean itself, \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\), and multiply both sides by n to see that \(n\bar{x}\) is just another way of writing \(\sum x_i\).

Final answer: substitute \(n\bar{x} = \sum x_i\) into the expression from step 3. The two sums are now identical, so they cancel to zero — and since n and the data values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) were never specified as any particular numbers, this holds for EVERY data set, no matter how many values it has or what those values are.

steps.explain: Put the calculator into statistics mode. On a Casio fx-82AU PLUS: press MODE, then select STAT (usually "2"), then select 1-VAR (usually "1"). This opens a table with an X column ready for data entry.

Enter all 15 Mathematics marks into the X column in order, pressing \(=\) after every value to move to the next row. Repeated values (like 15, 18 and 19, which each occur more than once) are simply typed in again each time.

questions.stem: Using the same class results (Maths: mean=16.13, \(\sigma\)=2.63; English: mean=15.87, \(\sigma\)=2.82), if a student scored 16 for the mathematics test and 14 for the English test, which is the better mark relative to the class results?
options: They are equally good, since both marks are below their subject's mean.
English, since \(z_{English} \approx -0.66\) is more negative than \(z_{Maths} \approx -0.05\).
Mathematics, since \(z_{Maths} \approx -0.05\) is closer to 0 (less below average) than \(z_{English} \approx -0.66\).
English, since 14 is a whole number below the mean while 16 is above it.
questions.hint: Convert each mark to a z-score using its own subject's mean and SD: \(z = \dfrac{x-\bar{x}}{\sigma}\). The mark with the z-score closest to (or above) zero is relatively better.
questions.solution: z(Maths)=(16-16.13)/2.63≈-0.05. z(English)=(14-15.87)/2.82≈-0.66. Mathematics is the better mark since -0.05 > -0.66.

steps.explain: Calculate the z-score for the Mathematics mark, using Mathematics' own mean and SD.
Calculate the z-score for the English mark, using English's own mean and SD.
Compare the two z-scores. A z-score closer to zero (or more positive) represents a relatively better result, even if both are negative.

Final answer: the Mathematics mark is only slightly below the class average, while the English mark is well below its class average — so Mathematics is the better result relative to the class, even though 16 > 14 already suggested this at a glance, the z-scores confirm and quantify it properly.

questions.stem: Data set (i) is the bar chart data set where the values 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 each occur exactly 3 times (n = 15, mean = 6.00, \(\sigma\) = 1.41). If 5 is added onto each data item, what are the new mean and standard deviation?
options: new mean = 6.00, \(\sigma\) = 1.41 (unchanged, since adding the same amount to everything cancels out)
new mean = 11.00, new \(\sigma\) = 6.41 (the SD also increases by 5)
new mean = 11.00, new \(\sigma\) = 7.05 (the SD scales by the same factor as the shift)
new mean = 11.00, \(\sigma\) unchanged at 1.41 (adding a constant shifts the mean but not the spread)
questions.hint: Adding the same constant to every value shifts every value — and the mean — by that constant, but does not change how spread out the values are relative to each other.
questions.solution: Adding 5 to every value shifts the mean by 5 (to 11.00) but leaves every deviation from the mean unchanged, so the SD stays at 1.41.

steps.explain: Adding a constant c to every value in a data set shifts the mean by exactly c, since the mean is just the (shifted) total divided by n.
Consider what happens to each deviation from the mean: if every value shifts by 5 AND the mean shifts by 5, the difference between each value and the mean is unchanged.
Since every deviation is exactly the same as before, the squared deviations — and therefore the standard deviation — are also unchanged.

Final answer: the new mean is 11.00, but the standard deviation stays at 1.41. Pitfall: assuming the SD also increases by 5 (a very common misconception) is wrong — a constant shift moves the whole data set, but does not stretch or compress it.

questions.stem: Data set (i) is the bar chart data set where the values 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 each occur exactly 3 times (n = 15, mean = 6.00, \(\sigma\) = 1.41). If each data item is multiplied by 2, what are the new mean and standard deviation?
options: new mean = 12.00, \(\sigma\) unchanged at 1.41 (multiplying doesn't affect spread)
new mean = 6.00, new \(\sigma\) = 2.83 (mean unaffected, only \(\sigma\) scales)
new mean = 12.00, new \(\sigma\) = 5.66 (\(\sigma\) scales by the square of the factor)
new mean = 12.00, new \(\sigma\) = 2.83 (both mean and \(\sigma\) scale by the same factor of 2)
questions.hint: Multiplying every value by a constant k also multiplies the mean by k, and multiplies EACH deviation by k, so the standard deviation is also scaled by k.
questions.solution: Multiplying every value by 2 doubles the mean (to 12.00) and also doubles the SD (to 2.83), since every deviation from the mean is also doubled.

steps.explain: Multiplying every value in a data set by a constant k multiplies the mean by the same k, since the mean is the (scaled) total divided by n.
Consider what happens to each deviation from the mean: if every value doubles AND the mean doubles, the gap between each value and the mean also doubles.

Since every deviation is exactly double what it was, the standard deviation (which measures those deviations) is also exactly doubled — NOT quadrupled, even though the squared deviations themselves are quadrupled (the square root undoes that).

Final answer: the new mean is 12.00 and the new SD is 2.83 — both scaled by the same factor of 2. Pitfall: thinking the SD scales by \(2^2=4\) (confusing it with how the VARIANCE scales) gives the wrong distractor 5.66.

questions.stem: Which of these lists of 10 numbers, where every number is either 1 or 5, has the LARGEST possible standard deviation?
questions.hint: For a list with only two possible values, the spread is maximised when the two values are as evenly split as possible (as close to 50/50 as you can get).
questions.solution: Five 1s and five 5s gives SD=2, the largest among these options (compared to 1.2, 1.2, and 1.6 for the uneven splits).

steps.explain: For data with only two possible values, the standard deviation is largest when the split between the two values is as even as possible — an extreme split (like nine of one value, one of the other) pulls the mean close to the majority value, making most deviations small.
Check the even 5-5 split: mean = (5×1 + 5×5)/10 = 3.00. Every value is exactly 2 away from the mean.
Calculate the SD for the even split.
Final answer: compare with the uneven splits (nine-one gives SD=1.2, eight-two gives SD=1.6) — the even 5-5 split has the largest SD of 2.00.

questions.hint: For a list with only two possible values, the spread is maximised when the two values are as evenly split as possible.
questions.solution: Five 1s and five 9s gives SD=4, the largest among these options.

steps.explain: As before, the standard deviation for a two-value data set is largest with the most even possible split.
Check the even 5-5 split: mean = (5×1 + 5×9)/10 = 5.00. Every value is exactly 4 away from the mean.
Calculate the SD for the even split.
Final answer: compare with the uneven splits (nine-one gives SD=2.4, three-seven gives SD≈3.67, two-eight gives SD=3.2) — the even 5-5 split has the largest SD of 4.00.

questions.stem: Which of these lists of 10 numbers, where every number is 1, 5 or 9, and at least two of them are 5, has the LARGEST possible standard deviation?
questions.hint: Since 5 is the "middle" value (closest to the eventual mean), using it too often actually SHRINKS the spread. Use only the minimum required number of 5s, and split the rest evenly between the two extremes, 1 and 9.
questions.solution: Using exactly two 5s (the minimum allowed) and splitting the remaining 8 values evenly (four 1s, four 9s) gives the largest SD, ≈3.58.

steps.explain: The value 5 sits exactly at the midpoint between 1 and 9, so including MORE 5s than required pulls values toward the centre and shrinks the spread. To maximise SD, use only the minimum required number of 5s (two), and put every other value at one of the two extremes.
With only two 5s, the remaining 8 values should be split as evenly as possible between 1 and 9 (four each), for the same "even split maximises spread" reasoning as the previous two questions.
Calculate the mean and SD for this list.

Final answer: compare with lists that use more 5s than necessary (e.g. four 1s/four 5s/two 9s gives SD≈2.99) or an uneven 1/9 split (e.g. six 1s/two 5s/two 9s gives SD≈3.20) — both are smaller than 3.58.

questions.stem: Which of these lists of 10 numbers, where every number is either 1 or 5, has the SMALLEST possible standard deviation?
questions.hint: Since a list "where every number is either 1 or 5" does not require BOTH values to actually appear, the smallest possible spread is achieved by making every single value the same.
questions.solution: A list of all 1s (or all 5s) has every value identical, so the standard deviation is exactly 0 — the smallest possible.

steps.explain: The condition "every number is either 1 or 5" allows a number to be 1 OR 5 each time — it does not require both values to actually be used somewhere in the list. So the most extreme (least spread-out) option available is to make every single value identical.
steps.work: \(\text{all values} = 1 \quad (\text{a valid list under the given condition})\)

steps.explain: If every value in a data set is identical, every deviation from the mean is exactly zero.
A standard deviation of exactly zero is the smallest value a standard deviation can ever take (it cannot be negative, since it is a square root of an average of squares).
Final answer: ten 1s gives SD = 0, smaller than any list that mixes in even a single 5 (e.g. nine 1s and one 5 gives SD=1.2, which is still much larger than zero).

questions.stem: Which of these lists of 10 numbers, where every number is either 1 or 9, has the SMALLEST possible standard deviation?
questions.hint: Since a list "where every number is either 1 or 9" does not require both values to appear, the smallest possible spread is achieved by making every value identical.
questions.solution: A list of all 9s (or all 1s) has every value identical, so the standard deviation is exactly 0.

steps.explain: As before, the condition does not require both 1 and 9 to actually appear — making every value identical is allowed and gives zero spread.
steps.work: \(\text{all values} = 9 \quad (\text{a valid list under the given condition})\)

steps.explain: Every deviation from the mean is exactly zero when every value is identical.
A standard deviation of zero is the smallest value possible for any data set.
Final answer: all-9s gives SD = 0, smaller than any list that mixes in even a single 1 (e.g. nine 9s and one 1 would still give a nonzero SD).

questions.solution: A list of all 5s satisfies "at least two are 5" and has every value identical, so the SD is exactly 0.

steps.explain: Re-read the condition carefully: "at least two of them are 5" is a MINIMUM requirement, not a restriction on the maximum. A list where all 10 values are 5 easily satisfies "at least two are 5".

questions.stem: An employer has 29 employees whose weekly salaries have mean \(\bar{x} = \$429\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = \$1.53\). The employer decides to give a flat $100 per week raise to every employee. What would be the change to the average ANNUAL salary paid to each employee?

questions.solution: A flat $100/week raise increases each employee's average weekly salary by $100, which is $100 x 52 = $5200 more per year.

Since every employee's distance from the (new) mean is identical to their distance from the old mean, the standard deviation formula gives exactly the same result as before.

Pitfall: it feels intuitive that "everyone got more money, so the numbers must be more spread out" — but standard deviation measures spread relative to the mean, and a flat raise moves the whole distribution without stretching or compressing it.
Final answer: no, the standard deviation does not change.

Data was collected on 100 adults comparing shoe size (ranging from 6 to 13) and height. An equation relating height (cm) to shoe size was found:
height = 127.18 + 4.84 × shoe size

161 cm; extrapolation (7 is outside the observed range)

questions.hint: Substitute shoe size = 7 into the equation, then check whether 7 lies inside [6, 13].
questions.solution: height = 127.18 + 4.84 × 7 = 127.18 + 33.88 = 161.06 ≈ 161 cm. Since 7 is between 6 and 13, this is interpolation.

steps.explain: Substitute shoe size = 7.

Classify the prediction.
steps.work: Shoe size 7 lies within the observed range of 6 to 13, so this is interpolation.
